title: Solomon's Palace and the Temple's Bronze and Gold
summary: Solomon spends thirteen years building his palace complex, including the great House of the Forest of Lebanon, a hall of pillars, the Hall of Justice where he judged, his own residence, and a palace for Pharaoh's daughter. He then brings Huram, a skilled bronze worker from Tyre, who casts two huge bronze pillars named Jachin and Boaz, a vast basin called the Sea resting on twelve bronze oxen, ten wheeled stands with basins, and many utensils. Solomon also makes the gold furnishings for inside the temple and stores David's dedicated treasures in its treasuries.
story: Chapter 6 built the temple's structure; chapter 7 adds Solomon's own palace and then the temple's furnishings. The placement of the palace account is telling. It sits between the completion of the temple's shell and the making of its equipment, and it opens with a quiet contrast: the temple took seven years, but the palace took thirteen. Some readers hear no criticism, since a palace complex was larger and the temple had been prepared for by David. Others hear the narrator raising an eyebrow at a king whose own house outgrew God's. After that, the chapter returns to the temple and completes its outfitting, so that everything is ready for the ark to be brought in and the building dedicated in chapter 8.
historical:
Solomon's building program in Jerusalem, dated to the middle decades of the tenth century BC, turned David's modest citadel into a royal capital. The House of the Forest of Lebanon, named for its rows of cedar pillars, was about 150 feet long and 75 feet wide, larger than the temple itself; 1 Kings 10:17 says Solomon kept ceremonial gold shields there, and Isaiah 22:8 later mentions weapons stored in the House of the Forest, so it may have served as a hall and armory. The Hall of Justice was the throne room where the king heard cases. The separate palace for Pharaoh's daughter reflects the status of an Egyptian royal marriage.

Huram (also spelled Hiram, and not the same person as King Hiram) is described as the son of a widow from Naphtali and a Tyrian father; 2 Chronicles 2:14 says his mother was from the tribe of Dan. Interpreters have suggested that she was of Danite descent living in Naphtali, or that the difference reflects two traditions. Casting large bronze objects required clay molds and a skilled workforce, and the Jordan valley between Succoth and Zarethan had suitable clay. These bronze objects did not last: King Ahaz later removed the Sea from its oxen (2 Kings 16:17), and the Babylonians broke up the pillars, the stands, and the Sea and carried the bronze away when they destroyed the temple (2 Kings 25:13-17).
cultural:
Palaces in the ancient Near East were centers of government as well as royal homes, combining throne rooms, reception halls, storehouses, and private quarters. Cedar pillars and dressed stone were marks of great wealth. The placement of the palace next to the temple also said something: the king ruled under God and near his house, and the temple functioned in part as a royal chapel.

The bronze objects in the temple courtyard had practical and symbolic roles. The Sea, a great basin about fifteen feet across, supplied water for the priests' washing (2 Chronicles 4:6). Its name recalls the sea that ancient peoples often pictured as chaos; placed in God's courtyard and resting on oxen, it may have expressed that the LORD rules over the waters. The twelve oxen facing the four directions suggest Israel's twelve tribes or the whole land. The ten wheeled stands carried basins for washing the offerings. The pillars Jachin and Boaz stood at the entrance; freestanding pillars flanking a temple entrance are known from other sites in the region. Their names are usually taken to mean something like he establishes and in him is strength, though scholars differ on the exact sense. Pomegranates and lilies, symbols of fruitfulness and life, repeat the garden imagery of chapter 6.
literary: The chapter is built from two blocks. The first (verses 1-12) describes Solomon's palace buildings in a compressed, summary way. The second (verses 13-51) describes Huram's bronze work in great technical detail and then lists Solomon's gold furnishings. The detailed, almost tedious precision is characteristic of building accounts in the Bible (compare the tabernacle chapters of Exodus 25-40) and shows that every part of God's house was made with care. Huram is described with the same triad of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge used for Bezalel, the craftsman of the tabernacle (Exodus 31:3), deliberately linking the temple to the tabernacle tradition. The inventory in verses 40-45 summarizes the bronze work, and verse 51 closes the whole building section with the note that the work was completed and David's dedicated gifts were placed in the treasuries.

outline.t: Huram the bronze worker comes from Tyre
The two bronze pillars, Jachin and Boaz
The bronze Sea on twelve oxen
The ten bronze stands and basins
The gold furnishings and David's dedicated treasures

doctrines.note: The careful craftsmanship, the washing basins, and the progression from bronze outside to gold inside show that approaching God requires cleansing and that the closer one comes to his presence, the more precious everything becomes.

The temple's imagery of the sea, oxen, lilies, pomegranates, and palm trees gathers up the created world into God's house. Many interpreters read the temple as a small picture of the cosmos, with God enthroned over all.
Huram's craftsmanship is described with the words wisdom, understanding, and knowledge. The Bible treats skilled work in metal, wood, and stone as a form of wisdom and a gift that can serve God.

words.note: Yakin, Jachin, the name of the southern pillar. It is usually understood as a form of the verb to establish, meaning he (God) establishes. The same verb underlies God's promise to establish David's throne, so the pillar may have announced that God upholds both the temple and the dynasty.

Boaz, the name of the northern pillar, usually understood as in him is strength or with strength. It is also the name of David's ancestor in the book of Ruth, and some scholars have wondered whether the pillar recalled him, though the text doesn't say so.

Yam, sea. The huge bronze basin is simply called the Sea. In the ancient Near East the sea often symbolized chaos, and Canaanite myths told of the storm god defeating Yam, the sea. In the LORD's courtyard the sea is a tamed vessel of water for cleansing, perhaps picturing his rule over all powers.

Chokmah, wisdom. Used of Huram's skill in bronze work (verse 14), it shows the wide range of the Hebrew word: wisdom is not only moral insight but expert craftsmanship. The same word described Solomon's God-given wisdom in chapters 3 and 4.

christ: The furnishings of the temple, like those of the tabernacle before it, are read in the New Testament as a pattern pointing to Christ's work. The letter to the Hebrews describes the earthly sanctuary as a copy and shadow of the heavenly one and presents Jesus as the high priest who entered the true holy place, not made with hands, with his own blood (Hebrews 8:5; 9:11-12, 24). The washing basins and the Sea, used for priestly cleansing, find an echo in the New Testament's language of being washed and made clean through Christ (Titus 3:5; Hebrews 10:22). Revelation's vision of heaven includes a sea of glass before God's throne (Revelation 4:6) and a new creation where the sea is no more (Revelation 21:1). The Bread of the Presence and the lampstands also find echoes in Jesus' words I am the bread of life and I am the light of the world (John 6:35; 8:12), though John doesn't cite the temple furniture directly. These connections are typological and thematic, not explicit predictions in 1 Kings 7.

hard.q: Does verse 23 get the math wrong, giving the value of pi as three?
hard.a: The Sea is said to be ten cubits across and thirty cubits around, which would make pi exactly three rather than about 3.14. Several reasonable answers exist. The numbers are rounded figures in an ancient building description, not engineering specifications. Verse 26 says the rim was a handbreadth thick and flared like a cup, so the ten cubits may measure across the outer lip while the thirty cubits measure around the body below it, and with a thick, flared rim those measurements could both be accurate. Ancient builders used practical measurements, and the text reports what was measured, not a geometry lesson. Most readers conclude that the verse raises no real problem for the text's truthfulness.

questions: Solomon spent thirteen years on his own palace and seven on the temple. What do the ways you spend your time and money say about your priorities?
Huram's craftsmanship is described as wisdom. How might your own ordinary work, done with skill and care, be a way of serving God?
The temple furnishings moved from bronze outside to gold inside. What does that picture suggest about drawing closer to God?
